learning_outcomes: Describe the purpose and main terms of Row-Level Security.
Use or interpret an appropriate PostgreSQL example connected to enabling row-level security.
Identify one edge case and select a safe way to verify the expected result.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on Row-Level Security. Its primary job is to help you design least-privilege access, secure connections, prevent injection and test row-level security explicitly. The listed PDF subtopics define the coverage expected here; work through them in order and connect each one to an example, edge case and checkable result.
content.why_it_matters: This topic matters because PostgreSQL systems must preserve correct results as data grows and more sessions or services interact with it. Practicing row-level security teaches you to make assumptions explicit, apply the right SQL or operational tool, and verify behavior instead of relying on a demonstration that only worked once.

content_blocks.title: Row Level Security
content_blocks.alt_text: Row-level security checks include the role, table privilege, policy and owner/bypass behavior.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Keep the problem small: design least-privilege access, secure connections, prevent injection and test row-level security explicitly. A PostgreSQL feature should be chosen for the semantics it provides, not just because it is available. Before executing a change, state the inputs, expected output and boundary conditions. The example below is intentionally small enough to inspect; it illustrates the idea but is not a substitute for a test against your schema and PostgreSQL version.

items.title: Enabling row-level security
items.text: Test as the actual application role with rows belonging to more than one tenant, including owner and bypass behavior.

items.title: Creating policies
items.text: Relate this point to row-level security: define the expected behavior, one edge case, and a query or check that would provide evidence.

items.title: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE policies

items.title: Policies based on roles and row values
items.text: Use a dedicated least-privilege role, verify effective privileges, and keep credentials outside course content and source control.

items.title: Testing isolation boundaries and understanding bypass privileges
items.text: Identify the rows and transaction snapshots involved; test a second session and document blocking or retry behavior.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Row-Level Security
content_blocks.expected_output: Enables row-level security and defines a policy for tenant-scoped rows when the table and application setting are configured.
content_blocks.safety_note: This changes security policy. Do not run on production without a reviewed migration and role-by-role tests.
content_blocks.run_instructions: DDL illustration only; create a separate lab table, policy, test roles and tenant IDs before use. Review owner/BYPASSRLS rules.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For a read-only SELECT or inspection command, no reset is needed. For DDL/DML, use a disposable database; capture the starting state, run the example, inspect the result, and ROLLBACK or drop the lab objects as appropriate. Do not use production data or credentials.
content_blocks.limitations: CodeLeaf currently previews HTML/CSS/JavaScript only; it does not execute PostgreSQL queries, shell commands or Python in the lesson page. Treat the sample as inspectable code unless you run it yourself in an approved isolated environment. Python examples require a separate isolated runner.
content_blocks.schema_assumptions: DDL illustration only; create a separate lab table, policy, test roles and tenant IDs before use. Review owner/BYPASSRLS rules.

content_blocks.title: Practical checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Security checkpoint: database privileges and row-level security are separate controls. Test as the real restricted application role; owners and roles with BYPASSRLS may behave differently.

task: Create a short practice artifact for “Row-Level Security”: explain its goal, show one example linked to “Enabling row-level security”, state the expected result, and include one edge/failure case and verification method. Use a disposable database or static artifact as appropriate.
hints: Start with the listed subtopics, especially “Enabling row-level security”, and describe the expected behavior in your own words.
Run or inspect the smallest example that demonstrates the behavior; do not add unrelated features before it is verified.
When the result surprises you, capture the exact SQL/error, check version and permissions, and change one assumption at a time.
expected_output: A reviewable note or query for Row-Level Security, with an explanation of “Enabling row-level security”, expected behavior, and a documented edge-case check.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying the example without checking its assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Object names, data types, privileges, extensions and data distribution affect database behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: List schema/version assumptions and test with a tiny synthetic dataset first.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a single successful query as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: A happy-path result does not test invalid input, concurrent sessions, permissions, recovery or query performance.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one negative/edge case and record the evidence that confirms the expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: Making a production change directly from a lesson.
common_mistakes.why: DDL, data updates, role changes and operational commands can affect data or availability.
common_mistakes.fix: Use an isolated lab, reviewed migration, least privilege, rollback/recovery plan and a second-person review for production.

summary: Row-Level Security fits into the broader goal to design least-privilege access, secure connections, prevent injection and test row-level security explicitly.
Use the curriculum subtopics as a completeness checklist: Enabling row-level security, Creating policies, SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE policies.
State the schema/version assumptions and verify one normal case plus an edge case before trusting the result.
